title: torch.compile mode="max-autotune" precision appears to be lower
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I'm sorry, this is going to be a terrible bug report, but I wasn't able to simplify the problem. 

I'm running a training run with a model that is compiled with `torch.compile`. The blue line below is loss with the `default` mode, the red line below is loss with `max-autotune`, the training runs are otherwise identical:

![spiky_comparison](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/22680696/224837823-788ccd48-6fb0-4099-9c87-46926dca134f.png)


It appears as if precision/stability is noticeably lower on the max-autotune training run. This is running on an RTXA600 GPU. The forward pass is wrapped in 
 `torch.autocast`, there are no graph breaks or warning messages. Max-autotune code is also noticeably a bit faster, so it is definitely doing something that the default mode is not.
 
 Feel free to close this issue if this is not enough info. I could also test more specific things or try to make a mini version to get to the bottom of this, but I have no idea what to look for, or which part would be relevant.

comments.body:
I reran this experiment with both variants,  `TORCHINDUCTOR_MAX_AUTOTUNE_POINTWISE="0"` , and `TORCHINDUCTOR_MAX_AUTOTUNE_GEMM="0"`, but behavior was the same -- so, most likely I didn't set these env variables correctly. Let me get back to you once I fix this.

Or is there a caching issue I should be aware of?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Those env vars wouldn't have effect until a recent nightly. Also, to be safe, removing cached files in `/tmp/torchinductor_{username}/` or running under `torch._inductor.utils.fresh_inductor_cache()` context manager would make sure that no cache is used. Autotuned cache shouldn't be used when autotuning is turned off, but bugs happen :-)

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Hi, sorry for the late reply, I've been having trouble configuring the inductor settings and nailing down the exact problem. 

So far, I've only found that the precision problems appears for both `max-autotune` and `reduce-overhead`, which speaks to `"triton.cudagraphs": True` being the source of the problem. 

However, I've not been able to confirm this via the options argument of torch.compile, the precision looks fine when I give {"triton.cudagraphs": True} as options dict (which looks like a problem on my end, from my reading of the inductor code it should work exactly the same whether `mode=reduce-overhead` or whether this dict is given).

I'll update when I find out more.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Thank you! Yes, `mode=reduce-overhead" should be exactly the same as setting {"triton.cudagraphs": True}, weird that it's not working.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Ultimately, I coulnd't really reproduce this issue on newer nightlies, it seemed to me like it was an interaction between `max_autotune_pointwise` and `triton.cudagraphs`. Seems fine with the new nightlies.

TLDR: The issue seems to related to [train.scheduler](https://github.com/reporter/cramming/blob/main/cramming/config/train/bert-o4.yaml#L20) in user code instead of cudagraph.

1. I can repeat the precision behavior using the provided command and user code. To simplify the debugging, I also tried (backend=inductor, mode=default) and (backend=inductor, mode=reduce-overhead), which [only differ by enabling cudagraph or not](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/_inductor/__init__.py#L128-L132). On “default” vs “reduce-overhead”, the precision issue persists.

2. To debug, I [set seeds](https://github.com/participant7/cramming/pull/2) for deterministics in the user code. With the modified user code, I can still produce the precision issue using “default” and “reduce-overhead”. I observed that `default` and `reduce-overhead` provide **different loss values** after each training step.

3. The user code uses train.scheduler called `budget-triangle2`, which uses [time.time()](https://github.com/participant7/cramming/blob/main/cramming/backend/optimizers/schedulers.py#L302-L308) for scheduling hyper parameters such as learning rates. After changing train.scheduler to `polynomial-decay` (not using time.time()), I observed that `default` and `reduce-overhead` provide **exactly the same loss values** for upto 3650 steps. See logs ([1](https://github.com/participant7/cramming/blob/deterministic/polynomial-decay-default-log), [2](https://github.com/participant7/cramming/blob/deterministic/polynomial-decay-reduce-overhead-log)). This result shows that cudagraph provides the same numerical results if other settings (e.g., learning rate) are same. The log after step 3650 changes since there are other hyper-paremeters (e.g., [batch size](https://github.com/reporter/cramming/blob/main/cramming/backend/torch_default.py#L175-L190)) depending on time.time() which are not modified. The issue may come from train.scheduler=budget-triangle2 instead of cudagraph. 

Happy to investigate more if @reporter sees the precision issue when disabling time.time() for scheduling hyper parameters such that the issue can be reproduced in a deterministic way.

4. When running with cudagraph, we see a warning message:
`UserWarning: Unable to hit fast path of CUDAGraphs because of pending, uninvoked backwards. Consider running with torch.no_grad() or using torch.compiler.cudagraph_mark_step_begin() before each model invocation`
This is due to a missing `torch.compiler.cudagraph_mark_step_begin()` at the beginning of training iterations. The user code always enters warm up branch (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/_inductor/cudagraph_trees.py#L1917-L1932), which means the real cudagraph is not actually running. Note: this does not change the aforementioned issues.

comments.body:
So, we're close to the 3-year anniversary of this issue, but after an email from @participant21 I did take another look. What follows is based on a longer model-based analysis that I have verified (although some residual uncertainty remains):

The issue does seem to be `cudagraphs`, specifically `cudagraphs_trees` in combination with gradient accumulation in older PyTorch. In PyTorch 2.10, this reverses and the `cudagraphs_trees` correctly produces a crash, while the `cudagraphs` default is inaccurately accumulating. 

Here is a minimal reproduction:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from collections import defaultdict

DEVICE = "cuda"
ACCUM_STEPS = 4
HIDDEN = 256
BATCH = 64


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(HIDDEN, HIDDEN)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(HIDDEN, HIDDEN)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(HIDDEN, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc3(torch.relu(self.fc2(torch.relu(self.fc1(x))))).mean()


def make_model_and_data(n_steps=ACCUM_STEPS):
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    model = MLP().to(DEVICE)
    torch.manual_seed(123)
    data = [torch.randn(BATCH, HIDDEN, device=DEVICE) for _ in range(n_steps)]
    return model, data


def accumulate_grads(compile_options=None, clone_hook=False, n_steps=ACCUM_STEPS):
    """Run gradient accumulation over n_steps, return per-param grad dict."""
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    model, data = make_model_and_data(n_steps)
    fn = (
        torch.compile(model, options=compile_options)
        if compile_options is not None
        else model
    )
    if clone_hook:
        for p in model.parameters():
            p.register_hook(lambda g: g.clone())
    model.zero_grad()
    for i in range(n_steps):
        (fn(data[i]) / n_steps).backward()
    return {
        n: p.grad.clone() for n, p in model.named_parameters() if p.grad is not None
    }


def max_diff(a, b):
    return max((a[k] - b[k]).abs().max().item() for k in a)


def accumulate_grads_instrumented(compile_options):
    """Run gradient accumulation with hooks that record aliasing evidence."""
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    model, data = make_model_and_data()
    fn = torch.compile(model, options=compile_options)

    incoming_ptrs = defaultdict(list)
    params = dict(model.named_parameters())

    def make_hook(name):
        def hook(grad):
            incoming_ptrs[name].append(grad.data_ptr())
            return None

        return hook

    for name in params:
        params[name].register_hook(make_hook(name))

    post_backward = []
    model.zero_grad()
    for i in range(ACCUM_STEPS):
        (fn(data[i]) / ACCUM_STEPS).backward()
        post_backward.append(
            {
                n: (p.grad.data_ptr(), p.grad.item() if p.grad.numel() == 1 else None)
                for n, p in model.named_parameters()
                if p.grad is not None
            }
        )

    return incoming_ptrs, post_backward


# =====================================================================
print(f"PyTorch {torch.__version__}, CUDA {torch.version.cuda}\n")


print("Step 1: Numerical check (4 accum steps vs eager)")
print("-" * 50)
eager = accumulate_grads()
print(
    f"  Eager baseline: fc3.bias grad = {eager['fc3.bias'].item():.4f} (expected 1.0)"
)

configs = [
    ("compiled (no cudagraphs)", {}),
    (
        "cudagraphs cudagraph_trees=False",
        {"triton.cudagraphs": True, "triton.cudagraph_trees": False},
    ),
    ("cudagraphs cudagraph_trees=True", {"triton.cudagraphs": True}),
]

# single-step control to measure baseline cudagraph noise
print("\n  Control: single backward (no accumulation) to measure baseline noise:")
eager_1 = accumulate_grads(n_steps=1)
baseline_noise = {}
for name, opts in configs:
    try:
        g = accumulate_grads(opts, n_steps=1)
        d = max_diff(eager_1, g)
        baseline_noise[name] = d
        print(f"    {name:22s}: max_diff={d:.2e}")
    except RuntimeError:
        baseline_noise[name] = 0.0
        print(f"    {name:22s}: CRASHED")

print("\n  Gradient accumulation (4 steps):")
# fc3.bias is input-independent, expected value  = 1.0
buggy = []
for name, opts in configs:
    try:
        g = accumulate_grads(opts)
        d = max_diff(eager, g)
        bias = g["fc3.bias"].item()
        bias_wrong = abs(bias - 1.0) > 0.01
        print(
            f"    {name:22s}: fc3.bias={bias:.4f}  max_diff={d:.2e}  {'BUG' if bias_wrong else 'ok'}"
        )
        if bias_wrong:
            buggy.append((name, opts, d))
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(f"    {name:22s}: CRASHED ({str(e)[:60]})")

if not buggy:
    print("\nNo gradient accumulation corruption found on this version.")
    exit(0)

print("\nStep 2: Storage aliasing check")
print("-" * 50)
for name, opts, _ in buggy:
    in_ptrs, snapshots = accumulate_grads_instrumented(opts)
    p = "fc3.bias"
    grad_ptrs = [s[p][0] for s in snapshots]
    stolen = in_ptrs[p][0] == grad_ptrs[0]
    reused = len(set(in_ptrs[p])) == 1
    print(f"  [{name}] fc3.bias:")
    print(f"    MB0 grad stolen (not cloned): {stolen}")
    print(f"    Backward reuses same output tensor: {reused}")
    for i in range(ACCUM_STEPS):
        val = snapshots[i][p][1]
        print(
            f"    MB{i}: incoming_ptr=0x{in_ptrs[p][i]:x}  grad_ptr=0x{grad_ptrs[i]:x}  val={val:.4f}"
        )

# --- Step 3: Confirm by cloning ---
print("\nStep 3: Clone-hook ablation")
print("-" * 50)
for name, opts, d_before in buggy:
    try:
        g = accumulate_grads(opts, clone_hook=True)
        d_after = max_diff(eager, g)
        ratio = d_before / d_after if d_after > 1e-12 else float("inf")
        print(f"  [{name}] diff: {d_before:.2e} -> {d_after:.2e} ({ratio:.0f}x)")
        if d_after < 0.01:
            print(
                f"    Cloning fully fixes it, res={d_after}"
            )
        elif ratio > 3:
            print(
                f"    Cloning largely fixes it, res={d_after}"
            )
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(f"  [{name}] CRASHED: {str(e)[:60]}")
```

----

So, in summary:

1.  Gradient accumulation really was broken with `triton.cudagraph_trees=1` in Pytorch 2.1. This actually matches the original look the of the accuracy issue, those runs still kind of  trained, but training was more noisy, given that the effective batch size was reduced.

2. Pytorch 2.6 did improve the situation, the same `triton.cudagraph_trees=1` now produces a crash: `accessing tensor output of CUDAGraphs that has been overwritten by subsequent run` , preventing a silent correctness issue. cudagraphs is correct on its own with trees turned off.

3. PyTorch 2.10 is worse again, while cudagraph_trees still correctly produces a crash, *the normal cudagraphs version appears to accumulate incorrectly in this scenario*! A manual workaround is `p.register_hook(lambda g: g.clone())`.

Ultimately though, my understanding is that cudagraph trees has been the default for a while, so the modern version of the problem that only appears when trees is turns off probably has not affected many users. The crash message with trees turned on is pretty clear and calls out https://<redacted-host>/docs/stable/generated/torch.compiler.cudagraph_mark_step_begin.html, and if this is used to mark only microbatch zero, but not the other accumulation steps, then cudagraph trees works correctly. 


P.S: A side issue is that cudagraphs (no trees) used to be more accurate in general for this example in earlier PyTorch. The repro above focuses on the scalar bias term, which is accurate everywhere in the baseline. But, even before accumulation, `max_diff=3.88e-01` is the maximal difference observed in the fully connected weights using cudagraphs in 2.6 and 2.10, which used to be ~1e-9 in eager and in PyTorch 2.1 cudagraphs.
